sections.title: About CETUS
sections.html:
About CETUS

CETUS is a desktop tool for Cue Exposure Therapy with Urge-Specific Coping Skills (CET-USCS), without virtual reality. In a controlled and supervised way it presents cues (images, video and sound) associated with the use of alcohol, tobacco or methamphetamine, in order to provoke craving and then habituate it, while the patient practises coping skills.

Important clinical notice. CETUS is an adjunct to therapy, for use under professional supervision. It is NOT a treatment on its own and does not replace clinical care. Cue exposure can provoke intense craving and carries a risk of relapse; always use it with consent, supervision and a safety plan.

Honesty about the evidence: rigorous trials of digital non-VR CET are mixed to null. The reference trial (Mellentin 2019) did not outperform CBT. Treat the results with caution. See Limitations and References.

sections.title: What is cue exposure (CET)?
sections.html:
Cue Exposure Therapy (CET)

CET applies the principles of extinction learning (from the anxiety disorders) to addictions: repeated confrontation with the conditioned cues, without using, reduces the craving response through habituation.

The patient observes the cue and lets the craving appear and, over time within the session, subside. The CETUS protocol follows Monti's coping-skills exposure model and Mellentin's CET-USCS app.

Scientific basis: Monti & Rohsenow (1999); Mellentin et al. (2017, 2019). The STOP button itself lets you halt the exposure at any moment.

sections.title: Behavioral mechanisms and evidence
sections.html:
Behavioral mechanisms

Each CETUS feature acts on a concrete behavioral mechanism. The evidence is presented with honesty: CET is a plausible adjunct, not a treatment proven on its own — its effects are small, mixed and debated. The app's metrics are descriptive and exploratory (small sample, no statistical inference).

1. Pavlovian conditioning and cue reactivity

With repeated use, neutral stimuli (a glass, a lighter) become conditioned stimuli that provoke craving. This is cue reactivity, the basis of the whole approach (Carter & Tiffany 1999, meta-analysis; craving ES ≈ +0.92). In the app: graded cue lists and the reactivity per cue in the report.

2. Extinction and within-session habituation

Repeated, unreinforced exposure (cue present, no use) weakens the conditioned response — Pavlovian extinction, observed as habituation of craving. The exposure is maintained until craving drops (Kiyak 2022, CET meta-analysis, small-to-medium effect, low GRADE quality; Powell 1993). In the app: craving VAS, live curve, configurable habituation criterion, % reduction and slope.

3. Spontaneous recovery between sessions

Extinction does not erase the original learning; the response can reappear between sessions (Price 2010). In the app: a spontaneous recovery metric (today's initial craving − previous final craving) and between-session trends.

4. Affect modulates craving

Negative affect increases craving; positive affect can reduce it (Heckman 2013). Craving during stress especially marks relapse, and a lower mean craving during exposure predicted abstinence (Schröder 2024). In the app: a gallery of positive images, controls to reduce the intensity of the cue, and mean craving during exposure as an exploratory risk signal.

5. Urge-specific coping skills (USCS)

Exposure is combined with active coping: the patient rehearses skills in the face of the cue (name the emotion → recall a consequence → recall a benefit → choose an alternative) — Monti & Rohsenow 1999; Mellentin 2017/2019. In the app: the guided USCS panel and its log.

6. Mechanistic monitoring

Acute change in craving does not reliably predict outcomes, so the habituation slope is watched as a marker — including the possibility that some adjunct blocks habituation (Ekhtiari 2022). In the app: the slope is saved and plotted between sessions.

Honest efficacy summary

The best comparative trial of a non-VR CET app (Mellentin 2019) was null versus CBT; pooled effects are small-to-medium with low-quality evidence (Kiyak 2022). Use it as support for clinical judgement, not as an outcome measure.

References: Carter & Tiffany 1999; Kiyak 2022 (doi:10.1016/j.addbeh.2022.107578); Powell 1993; Price 2010; Heckman 2013 (doi:10.1111/add.12284); Schröder 2024; Ekhtiari 2022; Mellentin 2019 (doi:10.2196/13793). Articles retrieved from PubMed. Full detail in docs/MECHANISMS.md.

sections.title: Craving scale and habituation
sections.html:
Craving scale (VAS) and habituation

Craving is measured with a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) from 0 to 10 at three key moments —initial, peak and final— plus periodic measurements (every ~30 s). The on-screen curve shows craving across the session.

The therapeutic goal is for craving to drop within the session (habituation). The app computes the habituation slope: a negative slope is what you want. The session can end automatically when craving stays low across consecutive measurements, or when the safety time limit is reached.

Scientific basis: in the VR-CET study for smoking cessation (PMC10980682), a lower mean craving during exposure predicted abstinence at 6 months, and craving was monitored down to two consecutive values at zero. Ekhtiari et al. (2022) warn that certain conditions (e.g. a single tDCS session) may block habituation; that is why the slope is recorded for review.

sections.title: How is habituation achieved?
sections.html:
How is habituation achieved?

During exposure the app declares habituation achieved when the last N consecutive craving measurements are ≤ T on the 0–10 scale. It is a simple, explicit rule, and it is configurable in Settings.

Parameters (default values)

ParameterValueMeaning
Low-craving threshold (T)2a measurement ≤ 2 counts as low
Consecutive low measurements (N)2how many lows in a row are required
Periodic VAS interval30 sfrequency of the periodic measurements
Session time limit20 minsafety cap

Which measurements count?

Only measurements taken during exposure feed the criterion: periodic ones and the peak craving mark. The initial measurement does not count — it is the baseline value — and the final measurement does not trigger the criterion either (it is recorded at close).

What makes the close reason "Habituation achieved"?

The criterion is evaluated after each periodic or peak-craving measurement during exposure. When it is met, the app shows the Habituation achieved notice on screen. The close reason depends on how the session ends:

  • Habituation achieved: the criterion was met and the session was closed with End session.
  • Stopped by the clinician: closed without the criterion being met.
  • Time limit: the safety cap was reached.
  • Stopped by the patient (STOP): the STOP button was pressed.

In other words, Habituation achieved does not mean the app forced the close, but that the criterion was met and the session was then ended.

Habituation slope (a distinct concept)

Apart from the binary criterion, the app computes and saves for each session the habituation slope (linear regression of craving vs. time). A negative slope is what you want. This slope is plotted between sessions in the Clinical report and is the main mechanistic indicator recommended by the literature. Watch it to detect the blocked habituation pattern that Ekhtiari et al. (2022) warn about.

Scientific basis

The rule of N consecutive low measurements reproduces, adapted to the 0–10 scale, the procedure of the VR-CET study (PMC10980682), which monitored craving down to two consecutive measurements at zero (0–100). The underlying principle is extinction through habituation with repeated unreinforced exposure (Monti and Rohsenow, 1999; Mellentin et al., 2017/2019). PMC10980682 also observed that a lower mean craving during exposure predicted abstinence at 6 months.

Adjusting the criterion

In Settings you can tighten or relax the criterion (for example: threshold 1 with 3 consecutive measurements, or a periodic interval of 20 s) without touching code. The changes are saved locally and applied to future sessions.

sections.title: Graded exposure and random order
sections.html:
Graded exposure and random order

Cues are ordered by appetitive intensity (rank), from lowest to highest, so that craving builds up within the session. Configure it in Configure cues with the ↑/↓ buttons.

In Prepare exposure you can enable Random order to counterbalance the order and separate the effect of the cue content from the habituation effect. During the session, use the ← → arrows to change cue manually.

Scientific basis: Mellentin (2017/2019) made the cues increasingly appetitive; the VR-CET study (PMC10980682) recommends counterbalancing the order of the scenarios. Personalizing the cues is the best-supported factor (Pollak et al., 2021).

Automatic cue advance

In Settings you can enable automatic advance: the app moves to the next cue after each craving rating (periodic or peak) and/or every N seconds. It honours loop mode and both modes are off by default, so they never interfere with manual exposure.

sections.title: Intensity control (shrink, blur, dim, mute)
sections.html:
Intensity control

During exposure, the patient can shrink, blur, dim and mute the cue. This gives them control over the intensity and is a form of self-regulation: an active coping skill in the face of the urge.

Each adjustment is recorded in the session timeline, because down-regulation is a clinically relevant behavior (it may reflect avoidance or coping). The clinician can review it alongside the craving curve.

sections.title: Urge-specific coping skills (USCS / CBT)
sections.html:
Coping with the urge: the 4 skills (USCS)

The Cope with the urge button guides four evidence-based, craving-specific coping skills:

  1. Name what you feel — identify the emotion and the physical sensation.
  2. Recall a negative consequence of using.
  3. Recall a benefit of not using.
  4. Choose an alternative action, a concrete one.

While you cope with the urge, the periodic craving measurements do not appear, so as not to interrupt the exercise; they resume when you return to the cue.

Scientific basis: the urge-specific coping skills component of Monti & Rohsenow (1999) and the CET-USCS app of Mellentin et al. (2019).

sections.title: Positive images (counterconditioning)
sections.html:
Positive images

The Positive images button temporarily replaces the cue with comforting content (pets, nature) or with the patient's own recovery reasons (photos marked as such in Configure cues). It is a form of counterconditioning and a way to evoke the benefits of sobriety.

Add images to the media/positive folder or mark them as a recovery reason so they appear here.

sections.title: Ambient sound and multimodality
sections.html:
Ambient sound

In Prepare exposure you can choose an ambient sound (e.g. bar noise) that plays underneath the visual cue to increase the sense of presence. It has its own independent mute control during the session. You can also use cues that are audio-only.

Scientific basis: the VR-CET study (PMC10980682) suggests adding sensory modalities (auditory, tactile, olfactory) to increase presence, which was only moderate with the visual channel alone.

sections.title: STOP button and safety
sections.html:
Safety: the STOP button

The red STOP button is always visible during exposure (also via the Esc key) and stays accessible even over the pop-up panels. When activated it: immediately halts the cue and the sound, dims the screen, and takes you to a calm screen with a breathing guide and the contact numbers (therapist, crisis line, emergencies).

Configure those numbers in Settings. The session is logged with the close reason stopped by the patient.

Scientific basis: Mellentin's app included a direct phone line to the therapist and supervised use; exposing vulnerable patients requires a safety plan.

sections.title: Sessions, logging and export
sections.html:
Sessions, logging and export

Each session is saved locally (no cloud): craving measurements, habituation curve, skills used, intensity adjustments, cue shown and timestamps. When it ends you will see a summary with the initial/peak/final values, the change and the slope.

On the patient's record you can view the between-session progress and export to CSV. For privacy, exported files use only the patient's pseudonymous code and the date (never the name).

The coping responses (USCS) are stored with their text and can now be exported to CSV ("Export coping" button on the report) and appear in the PDF report, using only the patient's pseudonymous code — intended for qualitative studies.

sections.title: Clinical report: metrics and scientific basis
sections.html:
Clinical report: metrics

The Clinical report (patient record → "Clinical report") gathers descriptive and exploratory metrics per session and between sessions. Important: the per-patient sample is small; these numbers carry no statistical inference (no p-values) and are clinical support under supervision, not an outcome measure.

Per-session metrics

  • Mean craving during exposure — the average of the measurements during exposure. A lower mean craving during exposure was associated with abstinence at 6 months (Schröder 2024, PMC10980682).
  • Cue reactivity = peak − initial: how much the exposure induces craving (Lütt 2026).
  • Within-session reduction = (peak − final)/peak: habituation within the session (Powell 1993).
  • Time to peak and habituation slope (negative = desirable; Ekhtiari 2022).

Between sessions

  • Spontaneous recovery = the session's initial craving − the previous session's final craving. High values suggest the learning is not maintained between sessions (Price 2010).
  • Trends in initial/peak/final and in mean craving during exposure.

In the "Craving per cue" table, the cue with the highest reactivity of that session is highlighted in bold (the most reactive contexts mark relapse risk; Schröder 2024).

PDF export

PDF (session) and PDF (full patient) buttons. You can include the clinic's logo and name (configure them in Settings → "Branding for the reports") and enable/disable "Include clinician notes in the PDF". File names use only the patient code and the date (no personal data).

References

Schröder 2024 (doi:10.1038/s41598-024-58168-7); Lütt 2026 (doi:10.2196/84156); Powell 1993 (doi:10.1111/j.2044-8260.1993.tb01026.x); Price 2010 (doi:10.1016/j.brat.2010.05.010). Based on PubMed articles.

Coping responses (qualitative use)

The PDF report and a dedicated CSV ("Export coping") include the four free-text responses of the USCS skills, timestamped and linked to the patient's pseudonymous code (no personal data). The CSV has one row per response (code, session, substance, time, skill and text), ready for qualitative coding.

sections.title: Patient management and cue library
sections.html:
Patient and cue management

Patients: create patients with a pseudonymous code (do not use the real name as the code). You can edit and archive patients from their record (archiving hides them from the list without deleting their data).

Cue library: in Configure cues you can add from the library, add files (several at once) or add a whole folder. Order with ↑/↓, enable/disable individually or all at once, and mark the positive images. The most effective approach is to use the patient's own personalized cues.

Media are stored in the media/{alcohol, cigarettes, meth, positive, sounds} folder. For video, MP4 H.264 + AAC is recommended.

Where data is stored

Depending on how CETUS runs, data and media are stored in the system user folder (Windows %APPDATA%\CETUS, macOS ~/Library/Application Support/CETUS, Linux ~/.local/share/CETUS) when installed, or next to the executable in the portable version (place a portable.txt file beside the program). First run creates the folders automatically. CETUS provides installers for Windows, macOS and Linux.

sections.title: Administrator recovery
sections.html:
Administrator recovery

Passwords are stored encrypted (PBKDF2 hash) and cannot be recovered. If you forget the clinician's password:

  • On the login screen press Ctrl+Shift+A to open the administrator dialog.
  • Enter the administrator key and you will be able to reset passwords, create a clinician or change the administrator key.

Important: change the default administrator key for security. As an alternative outside the app there is the utility tools/admin_reset.py.

sections.title: Keyboard shortcuts
sections.html:
Keyboard shortcuts

During exposure

  • Esc — STOP (halt the exposure).
  • ← / → — previous / next cue.
  • T / Shift+T — Size: shrink / enlarge (10 % per press).
  • D / Shift+D — Blur: increase / decrease.
  • O / Shift+O — Dim: increase / decrease.
  • M — Mute (toggle).
  • R — Reset the intensity (100 % size, no blur or dim, sound on).
  • L — Toggle cue loop (the arrows wrap around when they reach the end).

Global

  • F11 — full screen (toggle). Useful in kiosk mode during the session.
  • Ctrl+Shift+A — administrator dialog (on the login screen).
  • F1 — open this help.

Keyboard-only mode (accessibility)

In Settings → Accessibility you can enable keyboard-only mode for the exposure, designed for an adaptive keyboard with only Enter, +, −, arrows and numbers 0–9:

  • ← / → — change cue.
  • 1 / 2 / 3 — select the axis: size / blur / dim.
  • + / − — adjust the selected axis (highlighted on screen).
  • 0 — mute.
  • On the craving scale, type the number and press Enter to confirm.

An on-screen legend reminds you of these keys, the STOP button (Esc) is always available, and the mode also works in full screen (F11). In Settings → Keyboard shortcuts you can remap any action's key (STOP is locked for safety; accessible-mode actions are restricted to the adaptive-keyboard keys).

sections.title: Limitations and ethical considerations
sections.html:
Limitations and ethics

  • Digital non-VR CET is not a proven standalone treatment; use it as a supervised adjunct.
  • The evidence is heterogeneous: positive effects in open studies but null results in the blinded RCTs (Mellentin 2019; Garfield 2026).
  • Exposing cues can increase craving and the risk of relapse; maintain supervision and a safety plan.
  • Use only media with appropriate licensing (Creative Commons or your own) and review their clinical suitability.
  • The data are local; protect the device and respect the patient's confidentiality.
